questions.stem: Choose the correct article: I waited for ____ hour at the station.
questions.explanation: Article choice between a/an depends on SOUND, not spelling. 'Hour' begins with a silent h and starts with a vowel sound /aʊə/ → 'an'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: My brother is ____ MBA from Delhi University.
questions.explanation: MBA begins with the sound /em/ — a vowel sound, so 'an'. Same logic for 'an MLA', 'an SMS', 'an X-ray'. Test SOUND, not letter.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: He is ____ one-eyed beggar.
questions.explanation: 'One-eyed' starts with the consonant sound /w/ → 'a'. Same with 'a university', 'a European', 'a useful thing' — all begin with /j/ or /w/ despite starting with a vowel letter.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: ____ Ganges is considered sacred in Hinduism.
questions.explanation: Rivers, oceans, seas, mountain ranges, gulfs, deserts — always 'the': the Ganges, the Pacific, the Himalayas, the Sahara. Single mountains and single lakes are exceptions (Mount Everest, Lake Victoria — no article).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: ____ honesty is the best policy.
questions.explanation: Abstract nouns used in a general sense take NO article. 'Honesty', 'love', 'patience', 'truth' in general contexts → no article. We WOULD use 'the' if the reference is specific: 'the honesty of this man is rare'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: Mount Everest is ____ highest peak in the world.
questions.explanation: Superlatives ('highest', 'best', 'tallest', 'largest') and ordinals ('first', 'second') always take 'the'. Also ranks that are unique: 'the president', 'the Supreme Court'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: She plays ____ piano beautifully.
questions.explanation: Musical instruments take 'the' when referring to playing them: 'play the piano', 'play the guitar', 'play the violin'. Sports, however, take NO article: 'play cricket', 'play football'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: ____ Netherlands is a small country in Europe.
questions.explanation: Most country names take no article ('India', 'Japan', 'Brazil'). Exceptions — countries that are PLURAL or have 'Kingdom/States/Republic' in the name take 'the': the Netherlands, the Philippines, the USA, the UK, the UAE.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: ____ poor need our help.
questions.explanation: Adjective used as a plural noun to refer to a whole class takes 'the': the poor, the rich, the elderly, the unemployed, the blind, the educated. Grammar label: adjective-as-collective-noun.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: He goes to ____ school every morning.
questions.explanation: When the institution is used for its PRIMARY PURPOSE, no article: 'go to school' (to study), 'go to church' (to pray), 'go to hospital' (as a patient — British usage), 'go to bed' (to sleep). 'Go to THE school' implies visiting the building for some other reason.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: The complainant filed ____ FIR at the nearest police station.

options.option_text: a — used before words starting with a consonant letter
an — used before words with a vowel sound ('ef' for F)
the — definite article for specific or unique references
No article — abbreviations require no article in English

questions.explanation: 'F' in FIR is read as 'ef', which begins with the vowel sound /ɛ/, so 'an' is used. The article rule is governed by sound, not spelling. 'a' is wrong because what follows the article is the sound 'ef' (vowel-initial), not the letter F. All abbreviations read letter-by-letter obey the same vowel-sound rule.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: He has been subscribing to ____ Hindu for the past twenty years.

options.option_text: a — indefinite article before consonant-starting proper nouns
an — indefinite article before vowel-starting proper nouns
the — required before names of newspapers and periodicals
No article — proper nouns generally take no article in English

questions.explanation: Names of newspapers, magazines, and periodicals always take 'the' (The Hindu, The Times, The Economist). 'No article' is the most tempting wrong answer because 'Hindu' is a proper noun; however, publication names are a standard exception where 'the' is mandatory regardless of the proper-noun rule.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: The summit produced ____ European framework for climate cooperation.

options.option_text: a — correct; 'European' opens with the consonant sound /juː/
an — incorrect; chosen because 'E' appears to be a vowel letter
the — definite article only for frameworks already introduced
No article — abstract policy frameworks take no article here

questions.explanation: 'European' is pronounced /ˌjʊərəˈpiːən/, beginning with the consonant sound /j/ (as in 'you'), so 'a' is correct. 'an' is the classic examiner trap: candidates see 'E' and assume a vowel sound, but the article rule is governed entirely by pronunciation, not by the spelling of the first letter.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: ____ architecture of Hampi's ruins is a UNESCO World Heritage marvel.

options.option_text: A — indefinite article for abstract nouns not yet introduced
An — indefinite article for abstract nouns beginning with vowels
The — abstract nouns modified by a defining 'of' phrase take 'the'
No article — uncountable abstract nouns like 'architecture' stand alone

questions.explanation: 'Architecture' is normally an uncountable abstract noun and takes no article. However, when restricted by a defining 'of' phrase ('of Hampi's ruins'), it becomes particularised and specific, requiring 'the'. 'No article' is the most tempting distractor because candidates apply the abstract-noun rule without recognising that the of-phrase changes the reference from general to specific.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: ____ number of typographical errors in the final report was surprisingly high.

options.option_text: A — 'a number of' means 'several' and pairs with a plural verb
The — 'the number of' denotes a specific count with a singular verb
An — incorrect; 'number' begins with the consonant sound /n/
No article — collective noun phrases need no article in English

questions.explanation: 'The number of' refers to a definite counted total and governs a singular verb — here 'was' (singular) confirms 'The'. 'A number of' means 'several/many' and requires a plural verb ('were'). Using 'A' alongside the singular 'was' would be grammatically inconsistent, making verb agreement the key diagnostic clue in this sentence.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: India's ____ most prolific run-scorer in Test cricket has crossed 15,000 runs.

options.option_text: the — superlatives always require the definite article 'the'
a — indefinite article sometimes used with superlatives informally
an — chosen because 'most' appears to begin with a vowel sound
No article — possessives like 'India's' already replace 'the'

questions.explanation: When a superlative is preceded by a possessive ('India's', 'his', 'her', 'our'), the definite article 'the' is dropped entirely — 'India's the most prolific' is ungrammatical. The possessive itself specifies the reference, making 'the' redundant. This is a precision trap: candidates who correctly know superlatives need 'the' keep adding it even after possessives.

questions.stem: Choose the correct articles for both blanks: ____ Sahara is ____ largest hot desert on Earth.

options.option_text: The ... the — definite article for named desert and for superlative
A ... the — indefinite for the named place, definite for superlative
The ... a — definite for the named desert, indefinite for largest
No article ... the — bare proper noun paired with definite superlative

questions.explanation: 'The Sahara' takes 'the' because names of deserts, mountain ranges, oceans, and gulfs use the definite article — unlike names of cities or most countries. 'The largest' takes 'the' because superlative adjectives always require the definite article. 'No article ... the' is the key distractor for candidates who over-apply the 'no article before proper nouns' rule without knowing the desert/range exception.
